extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (prosecutors, litigators, and IPR practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Summaries of five Federal Circuit (CAFC) patent decisions from 2023 with the legal standards and practical takeaways that patent prosecutors, litigators, and IPR practitioners should apply in prosecution, litigation, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR estoppel: grounds reasonably could have been discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: The CAFC held that estoppel applies to invalidity grounds "that a skilled searcher conducting a diligent search reasonably could have been expected to discover."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proving estoppel under that standard rests with the patentee. IPR petitioners should consider which non-petitioned grounds might be subject to estoppel; patent owners asserting estoppel should plan how to meet their burden under this discovery/diligence standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODP determinations when PTA is present
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent has patent term adjustment (PTA), obviousness-type double patenting (ODP) must be assessed based on the patent's expiration date after PTA has been added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ODP is applied after adding PTA, a later-expiring patent with PTA may cause ODP against earlier family members. Terminal disclaimers can overcome ODP only if filed before the implicated patent expires. Practitioners should analyze family expiration dates and claim similarity when some family members have PTA and weigh the tradeoffs of filing terminal disclaimers (reduced term versus risk of future ODP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between PTA and PTE
rubrics_metrics.description: PTA (35 U.S.C. § 154(b)) compensates for USPTO delay during prosecution; PTE (35 U.S.C. § 156) compensates for regulatory delays in product approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior CAFC case law concerning PTE does not automatically dictate how PTA should be treated; statutes differ and should be analyzed separately when considering term-related issues and ODP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III standing and injury-in-fact for appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal to the CAFC requires Article III standing, which includes an injury in fact; this differs from filing an IPR (which does not require Article III standing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish injury in fact for appeal, declarations and evidence must identify specific, concrete, and imminent plans that would be affected by the patent (general assertions or vague expectations are insufficient). Arguments that a PTAB determination will have preclusive effect on unrelated pending applications are not enough because collateral estoppel will not automatically attach to PTAB priority determinations. IPR petitioners not currently facing infringement should consider standing implications for any potential appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement and undue experimentation (Amgen and Wands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that cover a broad genus (e.g., "all antibodies" performing a function) must be enabled across the full claim scope without requiring undue experimentation; the Wands factors remain the framework for assessing undue experimentation, and Amgen's guidance was reaffirmed by the CAFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification only discloses a small number of exemplars while claiming millions of possible candidates, that disclosure may be insufficient. Patent drafters should disclose structural attributes common to the claimed members or explain why certain screened items meet the claim and others do not so that skilled artisans can make predictions without 'painstaking experimentation.' Relying on routine screening that is effectively trial-and-error risks invalidity for lack of enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA public use bar elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), the public use bar is triggered when, before the critical date, the invention is (1) in public use and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'in public use' element is satisfied if the invention was publicly accessible or commercially exploited by the inventor; mere display at a public commercial event without confidentiality can qualify even if the public did not physically handle the device. The 'ready for patenting' element may be established by reduction to practice before the critical date or by enabling documentation describing the claimed invention. Practitioners should be alert to disclosures at industry events and ensure appropriate confidentiality or timing to avoid triggering the bar.
